passage:
My name is Lokesh. My first venture was a small tiffin delivery business, and it closed after eight months, with debts. I hid at home for weeks. Then Vishal, my old manager, asked me out for coffee and said, "What did you learn?" I said everything I did was too big, too fast.
So I tried again. This time it was one lane of the city, ten customers, no loan, and a page for every rupee. My hands still shook when I knocked on the first door. It didn't feel like courage. It felt like taking one step and checking my footing.
That was a year ago. Now there are ninety customers, and I sleep at night.

qa.q: How many customers did Lokesh start with the second time?
qa.a: Ten customers in one lane of the city.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when knocking on the first door?
qa.a: Shaky and frightened. It did not feel like courage but like taking one step and checking the footing.

qa.q: What did Lokesh change in the second attempt?
qa.a: Lokesh started smaller, with one lane, ten customers and no loan, and kept a page for every rupee.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Lokesh's failure?
qa.a: Vishal treats it as something to learn from, asking 'What did you learn?' over coffee rather than judging.

grounding: After a failed venture, a person tries again with less illusion and more preparation, in small doable steps.

passage:
Note from Afreen, team lead. Chaitanya missed the promotion round in March and told me he was "done trying." For a week his desk was empty by five. In April he came back with a plan: one certification module a month, feedback from two seniors, and another application in the autumn round. He was open about being scared.
Last week he asked me to review his practice presentation and said, "Where is it weak?" I had not seen him do that before. He isn't pretending the rejection didn't hurt. He has just stopped needing one big win to prove himself. I will keep meeting him monthly.

qa.q: When did Chaitanya miss the promotion round?
How did Chaitanya feel after missing the promotion?
qa.a: Discouraged and hurt. He told Afreen he was done trying, and his desk was empty by five.
One certification module a month, feedback from two seniors, and another application in the autumn round.

qa.q: How does Afreen see Chaitanya's change?
qa.a: Afreen sees that he is not pretending the rejection didn't hurt, but no longer needs one big win to prove himself, and plans monthly meetings.

grounding: After a rejection, a person tries again with less illusion and more preparation, rebuilding courage in small steps.
